title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 40 — Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges

content.overview: Section 40 governs a company making a public offer by requiring an application to one or more recognised stock exchanges and permission for the securities to be dealt with there before the public offer. It also ring-fences public application monies in a separate scheduled-bank account and restricts their use.
content.glance: Section 40 — Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges
content.study:
Section 40 governs a company making a public offer by requiring an application to one or more recognised stock exchanges and permission for the securities to be dealt with there before the public offer. It also ring-fences public application monies in a separate scheduled-bank account and restricts their use.

Statutory test
1. Public offer: the company is making a public offer of securities.
2. Stock-exchange application and permission: before the public offer, the company must apply to one or more recognised stock exchanges and obtain permission for the securities to be dealt with there.
3. Prospectus disclosure: where the prospectus states that such an application has been made, it must state the name or names of the stock exchange(s) in which the securities will be dealt with.
4. Separate bank account: all public application monies for subscription must be kept in a separate account with a scheduled bank.
5. Permitted use only: those monies may be used only for adjustment against allotment where the securities are permitted to be dealt with on the exchange(s) named in the prospectus, or for repayment within the SEBI-specified time where the company cannot allot securities for another reason.
6. No waiver: a condition attempting to make an applicant waive compliance with section 40 is void.
7. Default consequence: contravention attracts the statutory company/officer consequences in the section, subject to the current text and amendments (fine-only for officers after the 2020 Amendment).
8. Commission: the section permits payment of commission in connection with subscription subject to prescribed conditions.

Application
A company collects application monies into its ordinary operating account and uses part for unrelated expenses while exchange permission remains unresolved. Identify the section 40 defects, distinguish the exchange-permission issue from the money-use issue, and state the statutory consequence without importing a remedy not supported by the section.

Boundary
Section 40 is distinct from section 39: section 39 focuses on minimum subscription, application money and return of allotment; section 40 focuses on exchange permission and protection of public application monies. Section 29 addresses dematerialised form for public offers, while section 40 addresses exchange dealing and money handling.

sections.heading: Definition and legislative purpose
sections.body: Section 40 governs a company making a public offer by requiring an application to one or more recognised stock exchanges and permission for the securities to be dealt with there before the public offer. It also ring-fences public application monies in a separate scheduled-bank account and restricts their use.

sections.heading: Operative ingredients
sections.body:
1. Public offer.
2. Stock-exchange application and permission before the public offer.
3. Prospectus disclosure of the stock exchange name(s).
4. Separate scheduled-bank account for public application monies.
5. Permitted use only (allotment adjustment or SEBI-timed repayment).
6. Waiver conditions are void.
7. Statutory default consequences (current text).
8. Commission subject to prescribed conditions.

provisions.title: Companies Act s. 40 — Securities to be dealt with in stock exchanges

examples.title: Illustration 1
examples.body: A company proposes a public offer but has not obtained the required recognised-stock-exchange permission. The public offer cannot simply proceed on the theory that permission can be obtained later.

examples.title: Illustration 2
examples.body: Application money is collected into a general operating account and spent on unrelated expenses. That use conflicts with the statutory segregation/use restriction.

examples.title: Illustration 3
examples.body: An application form says the subscriber waives section 40 compliance. The waiver condition is void.

hypotheticals.question: A company collects public application money into its ordinary operating account and spends part while exchange permission is unresolved. What section 40 issues arise?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify the public-offer trigger, test exchange permission and money segregation/use, distinguish section 39, and state only the statutory consequence.

misconceptions.trap: Treating later exchange permission as curing a pre-offer failure to apply.
misconceptions.correction: Section 40(1) requires application and permission before the public offer.

misconceptions.trap: Using public application money for general expenses.
misconceptions.correction: Money must stay in a separate scheduled-bank account and may be used only as section 40(3) allows.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should section 40 be analysed on public-offer facts?
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE: Whether section 40 applies to the public offer and money handling.
II. RULE: Pre-offer exchange permission; prospectus naming of exchange(s); segregated application money; void waivers; statutory default consequences.
III. APPLICATION: Map each ingredient to the facts.
IV. CONCLUSION: State only the consequence supported by the current text.
